articles.title: US Marine arrested over murder of woman in Okinawa, Japan
articles.summary: Japan's government lodged a formal protest with the US, demanding that military officials take action.

blocks.text: A US Marine has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman's body was found in a hotel in Okinawa, Japan, local officials say.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the crime as a "brutal and heinous" robbery and murder. She said she had urged the US to "enforce stricter discipline" of its personnel.
Japan's public broadcaster NHK identified the victim as Yagi Anna, 39, and the suspect as Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma.

"We are actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine," the Marine Corps said on social media, extending condolences to the victim's family.
Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the woman's body was discovered early Saturday morning in a hotel in Naha City, the capital of the Okinawa prefecture.

"Such an incident is utterly inexcusable and fills me with strong indignation," Koizumi wrote on social media, adding that "incidents and accidents involving U.S. military personnel cause significant anxiety to the local community and must never occur".

The US Embassy in Tokyo said that it was fully cooperating with the Japanese government and local police. Japan's foreign ministry said it summoned US ambassador George Glass to discuss the incident on Sunday.
Okinawa is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja says the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.

"The fact that this kind of event has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military's efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective," he said.

articles.title: Yemen announces military campaign to reclaim land from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.summary: The Yemeni president's announcement comes amid an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.

blocks.text: But it is not yet clear whether this represents a new phase in the conflict.
The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis are engaged in a fierce battle with government forces for control of the region, as they seek to secure coastal areas and, by extension, the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.
Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz.
"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.
Away from Yemen, the Houthis are also trying to hurt the Saudis with an attack aimed at the country's economic lifeblood - oil.

On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east.
"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."

It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".
But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.
In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.
On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.
Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north.
Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition.
After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East.
The Houthis have launched a blockade of Saudi energy exports, which have already been squeezed by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Bukidnon Airport project displaces Lumad families, raises concerns over relocation site
articles.summary: The construction of Bukidnon's first airport is expected to improve transportation, tourism, and business in the province, but some in Indigenous families displaced by the project say they are still…

blocks.text: The construction of Bukidnon's first airport is expected to improve transportation, tourism, and business in the province, but some in Indigenous families displaced by the project say they are still waiting for promised services and livelihood support at their relocation site.

According to "Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho," the Bukidnon Airport is being built in Don Carlos town on nearly 150 hectares of land, and the government has allocated more than P3 billion for the project, which includes a 3,600-square-meter passenger terminal, a 2,500-meter runway, and an apron that can accommodate up to six aircraft.
The airport is targeted to open to the public in 2027.
Indigenous families relocated
Part of the airport site was formerly home to members of the Kirintëkën-Ilantungën Mënuvu and other residents.
Jessica Soho personally went to the area to talk to the residents.

Around 113 families are now living at a relocation site in Barangay Maray-Maray. Some families were relocated beginning in 2022, while others, including the family of purok leader George, were moved more recently.
George said his family had lived in Barangay Maraymaray, where they farmed corn, cassava, sweet potatoes, and fruit trees.
"Communal namin 'yang tinaniman ng mais, kamoteng-kahoy, tapos kamote," he said. "Blessing sa amin 'yon. Mga prutas, mangga, lanzones, rambutan. Ang dami naming tinanim."
["We planted corn, cassava, and sweet potatoes together in that communal area," he said. "It was a blessing to us. Fruits like mangoes, lanzones, and rambutans—we planted so much."]
According to George, residents had previously been displaced from the area in the 1990s and later returned. He said they eventually learned that an airport was being planned in the area.

"2016 narinig ko noon na parang sabi-sabi lang na tatayuan kami ng airport kaya 'di ako naniwala. Nag-away pa kami ng asawa ko. Sabi ko, 'Huwag kayo maniwala diyan kasi kuro-kuro lang ma-displace tayo.'"

["Back in 2016, I heard what seemed like just rumors that an airport would be built here, so I didn't believe it. My wife and I even argued about it. I told her, 'Don't believe that—it's just speculation that we'll be displaced.']
He said the situation became clear when construction equipment arrived.

The affected residents said they were paid for the lots acquired for the project. The government offered P320,000 per hectare, as well as housing, electricity, water, and a one-time cash subsidy of P25,000 per affected family.
Residents raise concerns over water, electricity
Some relocated families said their new homes did not initially have water and electricity.

Mila, a 71-year-old resident, said she received P320,000 for one hectare of land, although she said taxes and other expenses reduced the amount she actually received. She also received the P25,000 cash subsidy.
"Yung 25k, ginastos ko para malipat ang aming bahay doon sa ibang area. Pero, 'yun lang, maliit pa rin talaga 'yang 25k, Ma'am."
["I spent the 25k to move our house to another area. But still, that 25k really is just too small, Ma'am."]
She said the money was already spent on moving their house and that the promised utilities were not provided as they expected.
"Ang sabi sa airport, ang aming bahay ay package. May tubig, may kuryente. Libre lahat. Hanggang ngayon, wala."
["They said that at the airport relocation site, our house would be part of a package. There would be water and electricity, all for free. Until now, there's nothing."]

She said her family eventually took out a loan and bought a solar power system, while water had to be collected from a distant source. Other residents also said they have had difficulty getting water, particularly during dry periods.
The local government, however, said electricity had already been provided to the houses, with residents needing to complete the individual connections.
Engr. Eduardo Corotan Jr., acting municipal planning and development coordinator, said the government had also provided cash assistance.

"Regarding po sa kuryente, nakabigay naman po 'yung government sa kanila. In fact, lahat ng mga bahay do'n, meron kuryente 'yun. Ang kulang lang is yung iko-connect 'yung linya from the house to the line sa electric natin. Binigyan po sila ng cash assistance," he said.

["Regarding the electricity, the government was able to give it to them. In fact, all the houses there have electricity. What's missing is just connecting the wire from the house to our electric line. They were given cash assistance."]
On the water concern, Corotan said a reservoir was already available and that a program was being prepared.
The National Housing Authority (NHA) Region 10 also visited the relocation site after the residents' concerns were raised.
Engr. Clemente Dayot of NHA Region 10 said the agency's role was mainly construction and production.
Dayot said the facilities had already been turned over to the local government for maintenance and operation.
Residents lose livelihood
Aside from housing concerns, residents said their relocation also separated them from their farms and other sources of income.

George, who has been a farmer for most of his life, said he and other residents now have fewer opportunities to grow their own food. He said some residents have had to take construction jobs to earn money.
Another resident, Loloy, said he had not been given a house or the one-time cash subsidy. He is temporarily staying with a fellow tribesperson.

Catherine Cagampan, an administrative officer involved in the project, said the local government handled the purchase of the land and that the P320,000-per-hectare amount was based on the appraisal value at the time.
Cagampan also said some residents had claimed that their properties were part of an ancestral domain, but the LGU had asked for documents supporting the claim.
"Meron nagsasabi, Ma'am, na part sila ng ancestral domain. Pero, humihingi kami ng mga papers na talagang kasali sila. Pero, hindi sila nakapagbigay sa amin."
["Some are saying, Ma'am, that they are part of the ancestral domain. But we asked for documents proving they're actually included, and they weren't able to provide us any."]
The NCIP provincial office, however, said the airport project is within an ancestral domain.
"Ayon sa report ng ating team na pumunta doon, 'yung project ng airport nasa loob ng ancestral domain," Ronnie Bayaon, NCIP provincial officer, said.
["According to the report from our team that went there, the airport project is inside the ancestral domain."]
Questions raised over FPIC

The issue of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent, or FPIC, has also been raised. Benjie said their group had informed government agencies that the area was part of their territory and should undergo the FPIC process.
He also said they had not seen the Certificate of Precondition, or CP, at the time of the interview.
The Department of Transportation (DOTr) acknowledged an issue with the earlier FPIC application.
DoTr Director Eduardo Mangalili said the provincial government initially applied for FPIC in 2015, but the process did not materialize.
Mangalili said DoTr later applied again after learning that the agency itself needed to make the application.
"Yung mga submitted documents is no longer to be found. So nangyari po, nag-apply po kami ng panibago."
["The submitted documents could no longer be found. So what happened was, we had to apply all over again."]
Bayaon said FPIC is required when a project is located within an identified ancestral domain.

"'Pag identified ang ancestral domain, dapat magkakaroon muna tayo ng FPIC process para ang NCIP makapagbigay ng tinatawag nating certification precondition," he said, explaining that Indigenous communities should be informed about the project and its possible effects before deciding whether to give their consent.
["Once the ancestral domain is identified, we must first go through the FPIC process so that the NCIP can issue what we call a certification precondition."
Children face long trips to school

Residents also raised concerns about access to education. Some said children have to walk for up to three hours to reach school. Others said some students have stopped attending because of the distance and transportation costs.

Irene Dumpasan, whose children are among those affected, said the daily journey has become difficult for them. She said her children sometimes attend school only two or three days a week because of transportation and financial problems.
To help address the lack of a nearby daycare facility, daycare teacher Abby turned her mother's relocation house into a temporary classroom.
She said the original daycare center was left behind when residents were relocated.
Abby said she hopes a proper daycare center can eventually be built in the relocation site.

"Ang hinihiling ko lang, sana mapatayuan nila ako ng daycare center. Nag-worry ako kasi, malapit na akong mag-retire. Gusto ko mapatayo na 'yung daycare center, para may sustainable sila, para patuloy ang pagtuturo ko sa mga bata hangga't hindi pa ako nagre-retire."

["My only request is that they build me a daycare center. I'm worried because I'm retiring soon. I want that daycare center built so they have something sustainable, and so I can continue teaching the children for as long as I haven't retired yet."]
Supporters see economic benefits
Despite the concerns raised by some residents, other Bukidnon residents expressed support for the airport project.
They said it could make travel easier, bring in more tourists, and create opportunities for businesses and workers.
Bukidnon resident Elma said traveling outside the province can be difficult and expensive.
"Taga-Bukidnon ako, pabor talaga ako basta may improvement," she said.
["I'm from Bukidnon, and I'm really in favor as long as there is improvement."]
Vendor Von Santillan also said the airport could create opportunities for local businesses.

"Maraming turista na darating proud din kami na may airport kami, tapos marami pa makatrabaho, opportunities na makatrabaho - makapunta sa labas, importante rin sa ating mga negosyo kasi maraming bibili."

["Many tourists will arrive and we'll also be proud to have our own airport. On top of that, there will be plenty of job opportunities—people can go outside the province, and it's also important for our businesses because many people will buy from us."]
The Bukidnon Airport is expected to provide a faster route to and from the province once operational.

For the families relocated because of the project, however, concerns remain over livelihood, utilities, education, housing, and the implementation of commitments made during the relocation process. —JCB, GMA News

articles.title: Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism
articles.summary: Motion that has alarmed some Jewish members is passed by 1,022 votes to 813 at party’s annual conference in Brighton

blocks.text: The Greens have formally adopted a policy which equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.

In a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs, members voted at the party’s annual conference in Brighton to back a motion which calls for Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, to be “treated as any other form of racism”. It passed by 1,022 votes to 813.
The motion, which is now formal policy for the Greens in England and Wales, also calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel, “with equal rights for all”.

In earlier voting, an amendment ensuring other parts of Green policy were updated to take account of the motion was backed. Three other amendments, including one that said the motion should not be used to “pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions”, were voted down.

The primary motion, titled “Zionism is racism”, had been pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine, which encouraged non-party members to sign up to the party to make sure the policy was debated and adopted.

The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews …

“Zionism, as defined above, will be treated as any other form of racism, and this motion will be implemented by the anti-racism policy working group as appropriate and in accordance with its ordinary practice.”
Some Jewish Greens have said privately they are worried the policy could make it difficult for them to remain in the party.

A poll by the group Jewish Greens found its membership was split over whether to oppose the motion, while 81% said they did not identify as Zionist. The group is expected to comment publicly on the vote only after consulting members.

There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader, who missed the vote to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a parliamentary byelection next week, has justified the motion’s argument by noting the extent of the death toll in Gaza during Israel’s assault on the territory.

Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC: “Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.”
Four of the party’s five MPs have condemned the motion, as did Caroline Lucas, the former leader who was the Greens’ first MP.

Adrian Ramsay, who co-led the Greens before Polanski, said in a statement he would vote against it, as it set out what sort of Palestinian state should exist without taking into account the self-determination of Israelis and Palestinians. Siân Berry, another of the MPs, made the same point.

Carla Denyer, the Bristol Central MP who was co-leader with Ramsay, said the wording “risks alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people, including those who vehemently disagree with the Israeli government”.
after newsletter promotion
Another Green MP, Ellie Chowns, said the motion “risks fuelling division, and risks undermining the party’s ability to advocate effectively for justice and peace”.

She said in a statement: “Zionism is a contested concept with no single definition. If this motion passes, the party risks alienating many people, including in Jewish communities. Defining a highly personal and variable identity simply as racism risks reinforcing exactly the zero-sum politics we desperately need to get beyond.”

In a statement after the vote, the Green party said: “This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership. Our members value the ability to bring forward and decide party policy, and conference has now made its decision.

“The Green party is an anti-racist party and has consistently opposed the illegal occupation of both Palestinian and Syrian land, called for an end to arms sales to the Israeli government and spoken out fearlessly about the devastating situation in Gaza and the West Bank.
“Those positions remain central to our approach. So, too, does our deeply-held commitment to equality, justice and human rights for all, and opposition to racism in all its forms.”

The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the UK, condemned the vote. “The motion is antisemitic in its formulation and intention. By adopting it, the Green party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party,” they said.

“Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it.”

“The Green party would not presume to tell other minorities what their identity means and then use that definition to exclude them. Jews are entitled to the same respect. The party cannot impose its own meaning on a central part of Jewish identity, declare it racist and demand that Jews renounce it.”

articles.title: Would slashing migration tank the economy or reset Australia’s living standards? Canada may offer clues
articles.summary:
Annual population growth for the North American nation has slowed to just 0.5% – and the economy is ‘adjusting’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Would slashing net overseas migration “trash the economy” or deliver the necessary population “reset” to restore Australia’s stagnant living standards?
Labor and an ascendant One Nation have presented starkly different visions of what a migration program in the national interest looks like.

Pauline Hanson, the populist party’s leader, last month announced a plan to cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years by targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.
To achieve that reduction, net overseas migration (Nom) would need to turn negative for three years, the party says, before an ongoing cap of 130,000.
That compares with Labor’s longer-term Nom target of 225,000, and to the last official estimate of 292,000 in the year to March.
Tony Burke, the home affairs minister, said One Nation’s plan, if enacted, would “trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy”.
Hanson disagrees, and is quick to blame Australia’s high population growth over the past few years for the economy’s woes.
In a social media post, she said “vested interest [sic] are warning Australia could face a technical recession if migration is cut”.
“Australians have been in a per-capita recession for years. Their lives have been getting worse because of migration. Canada has shown living standards improve when migration is cut.”
For those looking for international comparisons, Canada has long been a type of sister country to Australia – similar size, similar culture, similar economy.
And the North American nation is in the midst of a dramatic migration adjustment that has flattened population growth.

Unlike Hanson, Canada’s policymakers have not targeted a specific net overseas migration level. Instead, they have rolled out a suite of policies to reduce the number of temporary migrants as a share of population from a peak of 7.6% in 2024, to 5%.

Canada is about halfway to this goal. The government has done this by reducing temporary arrivals, particularly international students, making it harder to extend stays, and giving some temporary migrants permanency.
Annual population growth has slowed from 3.1% in early 2024 to just 0.5% now.
So how well has Canada’s economy coped? And what does their experience tell us about how Australia should respond to growing calls for a more hardline approach to migration?
‘Canada’s economy is not broken. It is adjusting’
In May, the CD Howe Institute, a leading Canadian thinktank, issued a report on the country’s economy in a “lower immigration era”.
The title was “resetting expectations”.
Modelling by the report’s authors, Don Drummond and Parisa Mahboubi, estimated that employment in Canada could fall this year and the next.
Real GDP growth in 2026 may be no more than 0.5%, they forecast, and “little more” than 1% on average in the long term.
Falling employment would normally be cause for alarm, but Drummond and Mahboubi say this is actually “what a normally operating labour market delivers, given the demographic shifts underway”.
“These are not signs of a struggling economy,” they said.
“Canada’s economy is not broken. It is adjusting. Understanding that adjustment is a precondition for sound policy in the years ahead.”

blocks.caption: The Canadian economy has been ‘relatively resilient’, experts say. Pictured: Vancouver Photograph: Charles Mistral/Alamy

blocks.text: Nathan Janzen, the assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada, agrees with this assessment.
“What the population shifts have done has changed how we need to interpret economic data.”

The university sector has been hit particularly hard by the tighter migration rules. The government also provided exceptions to migrants working in areas of particular labour shortages, such as agriculture and the care economy.
But overall, Janzen says, “the Canadian economy has been relatively resilient”.
“If our population estimate numbers are right, we could have negative employment growth and still have falling unemployment. And the per capita economy looks like it’s getting better.”
after newsletter promotion
Canada’s recession and ‘cyclical factors’ at play
But economists warn against assuming Canada’s experience would be replicated here.
Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, says the first point to make is that Canada’s post-pandemic surge was far larger than Australia’s.
“While people here get excited about our post-Covid immigration, it was nothing compared to theirs,” Kearns says.
Even now, Canada’s population still sits 5% above where it would have been expected to be based on pre-Covid trends.
In comparison, Australia’s population is tracking just 0.2% above its pre-pandemic trend line.
“So the decline [in Canada’s population growth] has to be taken in context of the massive run-up,” Kearns says.
Canada also began its migration crackdown at a time of high unemployment in the wake of an aggressive series of interest rate hikes by the Bank of Canada.
In contrast, were Australia to crack down hard on migrants, it would do so with a tight labour market where unemployment sits at 4.6% and at a time of widespread labour shortages.
Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, says: “I don’t think you can just point to Canada and say, ‘Look, they did OK.’”
Ellis says there are cyclical factors at play that help explain Canada’s apparent economic resilience to its migration crackdown.
“It’s also because they are recovering from a recession,” she says.
The challenge of ageing populations
While Canada’s economy has, so far, coped with the country’s stricter migration policies, there is little appetite for them to be a permanent feature in a nation that remains open to immigration.
Canada, like Australia, is ageing. That means a shrinking share of taxpaying workers to fund the cost of providing pensions, aged care and health services to older Canadians.

The CD Howe Institute analysis shows that if the current era of low population growth became a permanent one, then Canada’s economy would be about 11.5% smaller by 2060, compared with official government projections.
“The implications for fiscal sustainability are significant,” the authors said. “This gap translates into structurally weaker revenues and higher debt ratios.”
Janzen says that, without immigration, “labour shortages are going to be a structural feature of the economy”.
“The view is that this will be a temporary adjustment, before we return to something more like historical rates of immigration.”

And while Australia may not want to exactly replicate our North American peer’s dramatic migration reset, there remain legitimate questions around how we can better manage a temporary migration program that has ballooned over recent years.

Ellis believes Australian employers have become too reliant on overseas labour, from chefs to workers in rural areas, and that this has come at the expense of training and hiring locals, even if it means paying higher wages.

“By choosing higher population growth with a high temporary component, we have made it easy for employers to look offshore any time they need to find someone for a job. There are definitely industries that have grown to be reliant on that,” she says.
“That degrades your ability and willingness to train your local workforce.”

items: Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

articles.title: Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal
articles.summary: Global campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuels

blocks.text: The hosts of the next major United Nation climate conference, Turkey and Australia, are facing criticism for being partners in a coal supply chain while remaining near silent on the need for a global deal to rapidly get off fossil fuels.

With the Cop31 summit in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya just a month away, the two countries running the fortnight-long talks have been accused by activists of a “vacuum of action” on plans for a transition away from coal, gas and oil – a key goal of many nations at the talks.

Preparations for Cop31 will kick up a gear this week with a small group of national leaders, including the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, expected to join representatives of more than 50 countries for a preparatory meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu.

Pre-summit meetings are typically bureaucratic gatherings, but expectations for his year’s event were elevated after Australia – which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31 – pushed to hold it in the Pacific, and invited leaders to attend, arguing it would highlight the plight of low-lying island nations.
Few leaders from outside the region accepted.

The Fijian government named five expected attendees – from Thailand, Antigua and Barbuda, Cape Verde, the Maldives and Timor-Leste – but some have since cancelled. They include the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, as Bangkok suffered severe flooding.

The meeting is being held just days after a New South Wales regulator approved the largest coalmine expansion in the Australian state’s history. Joint owners Yancoal and Glencore estimate the 19-year life extension for the Hunter Valley Operations thermal coalmine could lead to 809m tonnes of heat-trapping carbon dioxide emissions if it wins federal approval.

A report, by campaign group 350.org, cited UN Comtrade data suggesting the supply of coking and thermal coal from Australia to Turkey had been responsible for more than 75m tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since the signing of the landmark Paris climate agreement in 2015. It said the countries were now expanding their trade in liquified natural gas (LNG).

The organisation said this had continued while the Cop31 presidents largely ignored fossil fuels – the primary cause of the climate crisis – in public comments before the summit. Three letters to countries setting out the mission and expectations for the summit, two from the Turkish government and one joint letter with the Australians, did not mention fossil fuels. Albanese also did not mention fossil fuels in a keynote speech at Climate Week in New York two weeks ago.

Andreas Sieber, 350.org’s head of political strategy, said the hosts should be following the previous host, Brazil, in working on a roadmap to accelerate a transition away from dirty fuels. He said both countries should announce coal phase-out dates as a first step.

“Amidst the biggest energy crisis in history, it is extraordinary that the Cop31 presidency continues to ignore the central issue of fossil fuels,” Sieber said. “Rather than leading the transition away, both countries are still expanding fossil fuels at extreme rates.”

Australia has accelerated its clean energy expansion at home, but remains one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and LNG, with shipments this year expected to be worth more than A$140bn. The 350.org report said Turkey was Europe’s biggest coal-power generator and it had signalled it could expand its coal and gas power capacity by about 30% by 2035.

Australian climate change minister, Chris Bowen, has argued at previous summits that the world needs to move away from dirty fuels, including declaring at the Cop28 conference in Dubai that “the age of fossil fuels will end”. He told the Guardian on Sunday that Australia was a fossil fuel-exporting country, but acting on climate change was in its national, economic and strategic interest.

He said Treasury analysis had found Australia could have an impact on global emissions by becoming a renewable energy exporter. “Our trading partners are pursuing their own energy transitions. We want to help them do that, so we remain a reliable trading nation,” Bowen said.
after newsletter promotion

Turkey and Australia are sharing hosting duties at Cop31 in a unique agreement struck after a protracted standoff. Turkey has ultimate responsibility, including running a massive green trade fair, but Bowen has been appointed “president of negotiations” for the formal talks between nearly 200 nations.

The Cop30 summit in Brazil last year avoided collapse, but could manage only a voluntary agreement to begin discussions on a roadmap to phase-out fossil fuels after oil-producing countries countries opposed stronger wording.

Frustration over the impasse prompted 57 national governments to hold a separate conference on how to transition away from fossil fuels in Colombia in April. Turkey and Australia were represented at the Colombia meeting by senior officials.

Vanuatu’s climate change minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said it would be “deeply disappointing” for Pacific countries if Australia extended the life of a major coalmine as it led the Cop31 negotiations. “This decision sends the wrong signal at a critical time,” he said,

Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics, a science and policy institute, said it would be “interesting to see” if Turkey and Australia could set aside their “addiction to fossil fuels”. He said the Australia Labor government had approved 37 fossil fuel developments for export since its election in 2022, while Turkey under president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan seemed “fixated on prioritising digging up and burning coal … and establishing itself as a regional fossil gas hub”.

Cop31 will be held amid rising concern about the impact of what has been described as a “super El Niño” weather pattern, and after the UN Environment Programme warned the world would breach the 1.5C global heating goal included in the Paris agreement.

The UN agency warned every fraction of a degree of temperature rise would intensify destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion, and called for immediate and sustained cuts in emissions.

articles.title: JD Vance flexing Maha connections as he eyes 2028 election
articles.summary:
Considered Republican frontrunner for presidential election, Vance is cozying up to the movement – as it splits

JD Vance, widely considered to be the Republican frontrunner for the…

blocks.text: JD Vance, widely considered to be the Republican frontrunner for the presidential election in 2028, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement as some say it is shedding its grassroots supporters in favor of political and corporate interests.

The US vice-president has positioned himself as the inheritor of Make America Great Again (Maga), and attaching himself to Maha, which many in the Trump administration believe helped to win the 2024 election, signals a greater overlap between the two movements as the administration’s popularity plummets amid the war in Iran and rising prices.

More than two-thirds (68%) of rural Maha supporters said that Trump’s health policies have “had a negative effect or no impact on the health of people where they live”, according in a new AP-KFF survey that highlights the disconnect between the sprawling political project and its grassroots support, especially in rural areas that overwhelmingly supported Trump in the 2024 election. More Americans view the president and vice-president unfavorably than favorably, according to a January survey by Pew Research.

At the Maha summit in Washington DC on Tuesday, Vance traded jokes about memes and the “carnivore” diet of meat and fermented foods with Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the leader of Maha.
But Vance also highlighted his role in identifying what he says is fraud in Medicaid, Medicare and the Affordable Care Act marketplace – blaming it on immigrants, especially undocumented immigrants.

“We’ve found close to $250bn in fraud just since I’ve been leading the anti-fraud task force,” Vance claimed, though the administration has released scant details on who has been unenrolled from these programs and why the activity was considered fraudulent.

Vance said that “the states that administer the programs don’t enforce them at all”, claiming that undocumented people were receiving Medicare benefits, though there is no documentation that this is occurring. “Cut that shit out and be honest about your intentions. It’s about giving benefits to illegal aliens,” Vance said to applause.

Kennedy alluded to the more cost-efficient health systems of Europe, which have universal healthcare, to speak about the inefficiencies of the health system in the US, where costs have been “allowed to get out of control”. Vance seemed to point to the need for stronger regulation of the health system, saying that programs like Medicaid and Medicare are stronger when fraud can be detected – though the Trump administration has largely focused on deregulation.

Speaking at the event, Vance underlined “the politics that Maha is stirring up”, said Art Caplan, professor emeritus at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “I think Vance was there making a calculation. He wants to replicate what Trump did, get the Maha devotees on his side, not Rubio’s.”

Vance poked fun at secretary of state Marco Rubio, his closest political rival, saying Rubio “doesn’t have a great poker face”, which makes for “absolutely incredible” meme material. “Bobby and I are on a text chain with a bunch of the cabinet secretaries, where we’re basically beating social media to the memes,” Vance said, describing one image of Marco in a blonde wig after Dolly Parton died.

The second annual summit showcased the fracturing of the Maha movement, which has often been an uneasy alliance among environmental, nutrition and anti-vaccine activists, and political and corporate actors. The event appeared to eschew the former and prioritize the latter, featuring companies like UnitedHealth, Walmart and Anthropic, including companies with active business before the US government. Grail, an experimental cancer-treatment company whose approval is currently before the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), was a top sponsor.

Companies that paid $300,000 were given the option of speaker slots, as well as a private dinner with Kennedy and Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), according to reporting by Bloomberg.

The Maha Center, which organized the event, is one of many Maha-affiliated endeavors headed by Tony Lyons, a longtime vaccine critic, who has paid Kennedy $4m in the past year. Tickets were available for “Maha members” who pay $6,000 a year to Maha Holdings, whose sole board member is Finn Kennedy, Kennedy’s 29-year-old son.

“The Maha summit, I thought, was a giant conflict of interest,” said Caplan, adding that the “ethically disturbing” event appeared to be “pay to play” to access high-ranking officials in the Trump administration. Speakers included Oz; Brooke Rollins, secretary of the US Department of Agriculture; and Stefanie Spear, a top Kennedy aide. “Normally, you don’t get a chance to cozy up to FDA officials. That’s troubling,” Caplan added.

While Maha appears to be fracturing in favor of corporations, it could still prove a powerful movement for Vance, Caplan said: “If he can get half of what Trump got, even if there’s a split, he’s doing well.”

The strong focus on corporations was not lost on Maha activists. “Why are they excluding our voices?” Mary Talley Bowden, a doctor who opposes Covid vaccines and was reprimanded for stealthily providing unproven Covid treatments, said on X.

The lineup did not “reflect the issues that birthed the original Maha movement and drove voters, especially women, to show up and vote for this coalition”, said Kelly Ryerson, also known as the Glyphosate Girl. Some of the speakers “could not be less Maha”, she added.

Maha has been “captured” by the very corporate interests it sought to fight, Robert Malone, a conspiracy theorist who voted to restrict vaccines while he was a member of the now-halted vaccines advisory committee, wrote on his Substack – decrying the “incestuous nature” of Maha, where “conflicts of interest seem to multiply by the day”.

Kennedy, who has long railed against corporate influences affecting Americans’ health and wellbeing, was notably quiet about corporate power at the event. Instead, he praised companies like OpenAI, which has millions of dollars in US government contracts.

“Today, it would be malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or to make a prescription without at least checking AI,” he said, attributing the quote to OpenAI’s Sam Altman. Kennedy added that large language models “can give you a second opinion that is much better informed than any doctor in the country”. About a third (32%) of Americans consult AI for medical information and advice, though AI chatbots are inaccurate about 25% of the time.
“We’re never, ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us ‘trust the experts’,” Kennedy said.

“If somebody tells you ‘masks work, trust the experts’, AI may tell you otherwise. If somebody tells you ‘social distancing works, trust the experts’, AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that ‘a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, so you need to take it to protect your grandmother’, AI may say ‘it actually doesn’t do that’, So it really has the capacity to dominate us and free us from medical tyranny,” Kennedy said.
His “fringy science agenda was on full display”, Caplan said. If Kennedy aligns himself with Vance and Vance wins the election, “it gives him power to pursue some things that he cares about”.

Vance has long seen Kennedy’s faction as essential for Trump’s success, and he also spoke at the Maha summit in 2025. But fewer than one in four Americans (23%) view Kennedy favorably, according to a new survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center.

articles.title: US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say
articles.summary:
Suspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’

A US marine stationed on

blocks.text: A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.

US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.

The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported.

“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

articles.title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar
articles.summary:
Calyton said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but it also posed ‘a threat’ during his DNI Senate confirmation hearing

Donald Trump on Sunday named

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to serve also as the new White House AI czar.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
During his Senate confirmation hearing, Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger”, but it also posed “a threat”.
“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI.
CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.

In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.
The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – who he previously promised would be led by a “High IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.

On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed.
Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.

David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”.
Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton is ‘“a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.

articles.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.summary: Two residents in Mekelle tell the BBC pro-government forces have taken control of the city.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday
ByTeklemariam Bekiteditor, BBC Tigrinya, and Jack Burgess
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.

Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.

Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

blocks.caption: BBC map of Ethiopia showing the northern states of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. The regional capital of Mekelle is labelled in Tigray and the national capital Addis Ababa is also located near the centre of the country and just outside the three northern states. Eritrea is shown to the north, borderin…

blocks.text: On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.

Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.

The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Debris found after medical plane carrying six people went missing off Nantucket
articles.summary:
Six passengers and crew on board still unaccounted for after medical transport plane vanishes over Atlantic, officials say

Researches found debris from a medical transport plane that was…

blocks.text: Researches found debris from a medical transport plane that was carrying six people when it vanished over the Atlantic early on Saturday during a flight from Bermuda to Boston, the US Coast Guard said.

A statement from the Coast Guard issued on Saturday evening said crews searching off the coast of the Massachusetts island Nantucket “located a debris field confirmed to be from the aircraft”, described as an air ambulance.

Six passengers and crew on board were still unaccounted for at the time of the debris field’s discovery, a spokesperson for the Coast Guard said. Boats, planes and helicopters were launched after flight controllers lost contact with the air ambulance.
Air traffic controllers had difficulty communicating with the flight in its final moments.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12.46am. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
According to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, the pilot’s response was not audible.

The air ambulance – a Gulfstream G100 – took off from Bermuda late on Saturday, carrying a patient, a family member and a four-person crew. The patient and family member were identified as citizens of Bermuda. The crew was identified as Canadian citizens, though the names of the people on board the flight were not immediately released.

As it neared Nantucket, the plane reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions. Data from the website FlightAware shows the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes and disappeared from radar shortly after at about 1am local time.
The Coast Guard said on Saturday evening that its William Sparling cutter boat would continue searching for those onboard the air ambulance through the night.
The agency reported that its crews searched roughtly 1,644 sq miles (4,258 sq km) for the aircraft in about 27 hours.
“Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night.”
Bermudian government officials said they had been in touch with the passengers’ families.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time,” Bermuda premier David Burt in a statement. “We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

articles.title: After a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House race
articles.summary:
In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat

On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state, Laura…

blocks.text: On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state, Laura Oltmann, a 41-year-old dietitian, had barely clocked in when an unfamiliar overhead announcement echoed through the hospital.
“We get overhead pages for different types of emergencies. But this one, we don’t get very often,” recalled Oltmann.

Doctors, nurses and staff began guessing what could have happened. Perhaps it was a train derailment. Maybe a major highway crash. As the speculation grew, so did the uncertainty. Staff started calling one another. The answer shook them all. “Someone mentioned there had been an explosion at this plant, and that we were probably going to be getting some patients from there,” Oltmann said.

Forty miles south, in the port city of Longview, residents had awakened to a thunderous boom. At approximately 7.18am, as workers changed shifts at a paper mill company, Nippon Dynawave Packaging, a tank of white liquor, a caustic chemical used in the paper-making process, imploded. Hours passed with no explanation of what had caused it or how it could have happened at all, and suspicion began to brew.
With roughly a thousand people working at the mill, thousands more were waiting for a phone call. Parents called children. Wives called husbands. Grandparents called grandchildren.

blocks.caption: Damage at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging mill in Longview, Washington, after an implosion on 26 May. Photograph: Karen Ducey/The Seattle Times/AP

blocks.text: “For those that did not get that response,” said Jeff Wilson, a Republican state senator representing Longview, who also sits as the port commissioner, “all they got was silence.” In the end, 11 people were killed in one of Washington state’s deadliest industrial accidents in nearly a century.

Nowhere was that impact felt more deeply than in Longview itself, a working-class city of about 38,000 people whose economy and identity have long been tied to the paper industry, shipping and logging. For generations, families have depended on the mills for their livelihoods. The disaster struck at something the city had long regarded as permanent: the mills where generations had gone to work, and helped many send their children to college or put down a down payment on a home.

The implosion rippled through nearly every corner of a community affected by mill closures and economic change. Those concerns will likely have an impact at the ballot box. As summer turned toward fall and the leaves along the Columbia River began to turn yellow, memorial services gave way to campaign rallies. The same communities that had gathered around grieving families were preparing for one of the country’s most closely watched House races in November.

Nearly two months after the implosion, on 8 July, Wilson still spoke first about the workers, the funerals he had attended, the families and the co-workers who ran toward danger looking for one another. He recalled brothers Tyler and Brad Covington, 27 and 29; he said: “They went to work together. And then they died together.”

Before entering politics, Wilson spent more than 23 years cleaning tanks at the Nippon Dynawave mill. In the aftermath of the tragedy, he worked routinely with Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as local, state and federal officials responded to the disaster, his role in Olympia intersecting with hers in Washington.

blocks.caption: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez speaks to reporters. Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images

blocks.text: Though he declined to endorse her re-election, Wilson credited the Democratic congresswoman with being “present and accountable” and praised her for asking questions rather than “rubber-stamping anything”.

For a community divided by many of the same political forces pulling at the rest of the country, the disaster briefly created a sense of togetherness, as the whole community grieved the deaths of many of their neighbor and family members.

“Natural disasters will tend to bring people together,” said Mark Alan Smith, a political science professor at the University of Washington who studies American politics and religion. “It’s something people can unify around … across race and class and other divisions.”

On 4 August, Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican state senator John Braun advanced from a field of nine to face off for the district’s congressional seat in November. Braun finished first with about 39.7% of the vote to Gluesenkamp Perez’s 36.4%. Brent Hennrich, the progressive Democrat who argued that Gluesenkamp Perez no longer represented many of her party’s voters, took 16.7%.

The results exposed the competing pressures facing Gluesenkamp Perez heading into the general election. Braun finished ahead of the incumbent, while Hennrich’s showing demonstrated the size of the progressive bloc she will have to contend with in November. Many of those voters remain angry over parts of her vote on the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) Act (which would require proof of citizenship to vote), ICE funding and a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity.

When asked about those direct criticisms of the congresswoman – whom many on the left feel has drifted from the party – her campaign responded with a written statement to the Guardian that cast her independence as the reason south-west Washington should return her to office. “DC has enough career politicians following national agendas,” said campaign manager Timothy Gowen. “Southwest Washington deserves an independent representative who delivers real results. Marie will always be loyal to her district first.” The statement did not address questions about her voting record or the primary result.

blocks.caption: John Braun at the capitol in Olympia last year. Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/AP

blocks.text: The race stretches far beyond Longview and the nearby city of Battle Ground. Washington’s third congressional district runs from the Pacific coast through the timber towns of the lower Columbia and inland farm country to Vancouver and the fast-growing suburbs north of Portland. Logging, paper mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life across much of it, while its politics pull hard in opposite directions.

That geography has forced Gluesenkamp Perez to build an unusual coalition. Her political survival has depended partly on voters who do not ordinarily identify with Democrats, including moderates and conservatives drawn to her emphasis on the trades, guns and independence from her party. But that same positioning has alienated Democrats who believe she has moved too far from them.

“Two years ago, people reported having to hold their nose and vote for her, because she was better than [former opponent and one-time counter-intelligence official] Joe Kent,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. “But now we’re in a situation where I’m hearing from so many people that even if she wins the primary, they will not vote for her. And the frustration is real. I’m feeling that personally.”

Thea Zaine, chair of the 20th Legislative District Democrats, speaks for the bloc of progressive Democrats whose discontent showed up in the primary returns. Her organization was the only Democratic party body in the district to endorse Hennrich.

“We believe in protecting immigrants. She’s voted to give more money to ICE,” Zaine said. “She voted to give funding to wars in Iran. And she takes money from Aipac, and she’s voted to fund the genocide in Gaza. She voted against the war powers resolution to rein in Trump.”
For Zaine, those votes have made the choice straightforward. But not every young, left-leaning voter who shares her frustration has reached the same conclusion.
Tanner Manley, 25, an incoming law student who lives near Vancouver and describes himself as left-leaning, shares much of the critique. He plans to vote for Gluesenkamp Perez anyway.

blocks.caption: Protesters gather in front of the Henry M Jackson federal building in Seattle. Photograph: Rio Giancarlo/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Of course, I wish more progressive candidates were viable here, and that Marie would take a clear moral stand on Israel and reject Aipac funding the way she refuses corporate Pac money,” he said. “In another race with different options, I’d likely support a different candidate.”

What keeps Manley with her is closer to home. After the Longview disaster, the US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the independent federal agency investigating the tank failure at the Longview paper plant, faced elimination under the administration’s proposed budget. In June, Gluesenkamp Perez backed an amendment restoring $14m for the agency, which passed the House appropriations committee with Republican support.
“That might not satisfy progressives watching from the other side of the country,” Manley said, “but try telling people in this district that that kind of fight in Congress doesn’t matter.”

Neither candidate’s campaign has made the Longview tragedy a centerpiece of the race. A recent poll underscores how little room both candidates have: the survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided.
Smith, of the University of Washington, said events that bring communities together can be difficult to translate into partisan advantage.
“In order for something like that to affect how people vote, somebody has to channel it,” Smith said. “It’s hard to channel anything where everybody agrees.”

That could change, he said, “if you can somehow link your opponent to some negative aspect” of the event. So far, neither campaign has done so. And Wilson praised Gluesenkamp Perez’s handling of the disaster.
“She’s been representing, you know, from the federal angle, well on this,” he said.

The response also fit the political identity Gluesenkamp Perez has cultivated in south-west Washington, where she has emphasized the trades and the economic pressures facing rural and working-class communities. In an interview with OPB, she described watching the decline of industries that have long sustained towns across the region.
“Mill after mill close in our region,” she said. “It’s just got people really at high anxiety levels.”

A recent poll underscores how little room both House candidates have. The survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided.
About three miles north of Nippon Dynawave, at the Pentecostal church where Ron Peterson is pastor, the disaster remains part of the community’s memory.
For Peterson, 38, the tragedy had briefly brought together people who otherwise disagreed about much else. But when I asked him about politics, he drew a distinction.

blocks.caption: A vigil for the victims of the explosion. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters

blocks.text: “We don’t win politically,” he said. “We win spiritually.”

A few miles south, and across a district where the divisions are not only political, Chydell Armijo, 35, mother of two, was thinking about something more immediate. She had little enthusiasm for either political party. What worried her was whether people like her could still build a stable life: whether a small business could survive, whether her children could find opportunity and whether working people could still move up.
“I honestly feel like everybody is struggling,” Armijo said. “There is no such thing as middle class any more.”
For all the attention on which party will control this congressional seat after November, Armijo saw a divide that would remain regardless of who won.
“Our economic system has become difficult, in many ways, for us to climb,” she said.

articles.title: For advocates, CHED’s openness to lived names policy brings hope
articles.summary: There is no blanket policy yet that would allow transgender and queer students to be recognized by their lived names during graduation rites

blocks.text: PRIDE. Members of the LGBTQ+ community gather at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City for the annual Pride March, June 28, 2025.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
There is no blanket policy yet that would allow transgender and queer students to be recognized by their lived names during graduation rites

items: The Commission on Higher Education is open to discussing a policy that would allow transgender students to use their lived names during graduation ceremonies, which advocates view positively.
Advocates emphasize the need for comprehensive legislation, such as the SOGIESC bill, to promote inclusivity and address discrimination.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) has expressed openness to discussing a policy that would allow transgender and queer college students to use their lived names during graduation ceremonies, bringing hope to advocates.
Lived names are the chosen names of individuals used in daily life, different from their legal names.

“CHED actually does not see any legal impediment. CHED is, in fact, very open to a discussion regarding this,” Makati City 1st District Representative Monique Lagdameo said on September 23, during the plenary deliberations on the commission’s proposed 2027 budget in the House of Representatives.

Akbayan Representative Perci Cendaña brought the matter to the plenary after the Polytechnic University of the Philippines committed to allow its trans graduates to be recognized using their lived names during commencement exercises.

A similar policy was also implemented in other institutions such as the University of the Philippines, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, Philippine Normal University, De La Salle University, and Ateneo de Manila University, according to Cendaña.
However, Lagdameo, who spoke on behalf of CHED as its budget sponsor, noted that official records would still reflect the students’ names based on their birth certificates.

“I think maganda rin po itong way (this is a good way) for us to really navigate, how to literally open our minds and open our government into accepting and fully recognizing trans people and queer individuals with their lived name as well,” said Jira Samson, 22, who was not permitted to use her lived name during her graduation ceremony.
In an interview with Rappler, Samson, who recently graduated from Batangas State University, said the possible policy may benefit her “trans-siblings” who have just started their college journey.
Francheska Louise Chua, a 26-year-old medical student, said the openness to talks is a “big step forward” that could make a difference in the future.

But worries persist. “We are all scared, because as much as it is a conversation, hindi pa siya (it’s still not) undergoing implementation. So there’s still a big chance [a policy will not be issued],” she told Rappler.
“Obviously, there will be voters for yes or no, and it’s a long process…. This openness to conversations such as this is already a big step. So, as much as we are scared, we are still hopeful.”

Samson said university staff were sympathetic to her request to be recognized using her lived name during their graduation. But it was not granted as there was no specific CHED policy allowing for it to happen.
She noted that being recognized using one’s lived name is part of the gender-affirming and transitioning process of transgender and queer people, which must be respected.
Other than the recognition of lived names, Samson said dress code policies should be inclusive for LGBTQ+ students, and gender-responsive education must be strictly implemented.

“Ano ba naman po ‘yong i-recognize kami ng graduation, eh kung buong taon kami nakakaranas ng discrimination? Wala rin, ‘di ba?” she said. (What’s the use of being recognized by our lived name during graduation, if the whole year we experience discrimination? It would be useless, right?)
Recently, at Batangas State University, a transgender student was allegedly harassed by a security official as she was told to take off her bra in public because of dress code violations.

“It is just sad to note [that] such [a] university has not communicated this incident to CHED. But now that you have brought it to the attention of CHED, please know CHED will look into it and address the same,” Lagdameo told Cendaña during the September 23 budget deliberations.
CHED maintained it has existing memorandum orders recognizing the rights of students, as well as observing inclusivity in campuses.
Chua, who is a beauty queen, also conducts awareness campaigns about the LGBTQ+ community in Iloilo province.

But more than that, she believes the passage of a bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics (SOGIESC) “will really promote genuine inclusivity.”
In the 20th Congress, there are seven pending SOGIESC bills in the House, and two in the Senate.
The proposed measure has been languishing in Congress for over two decades already. (READ: Why is it taking so long to pass the SOGIESC bill?)

Ahead of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address in July, his son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, said he would be “happy to pass it when one comes to light,” but added that consultations are needed on whether or not it should be a priority bill.

blocks.caption: For advocates, CHED’s openness to lived names policy brings hope

blocks.text: Another pending proposal is the lived identities recognition bill, which seeks to allow transgender, intersex, and non-binary people to amend legal documents, specifically for name change and gender recognition, without going to court. – Rappler.com
