articles.title: Latvia election: Pro-Ukraine PM Kulbergs set to retain power after historic victory for his United List party
articles.summary: Latvia's prime minister looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.

image.caption: Centrist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (right) is the favorite, but his coalition is expected to emerge weakenedImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election.
The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition.
What do the results show?
With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said.

Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears

An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.
Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.
Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones. Despite his party leading opinion polls, his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.
Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.
Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.
Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats
German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace
Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.
Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.
Once ballots are fully counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.
Estonia and Latvia: Life on NATO's eastern edge

articles.title: Ukraine to step up oil attacks as Russia hits Kyiv bridges
articles.summary: As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.
articles.byline: Nik Martin, Wesley Dockery, Dharvi Vaid Dhulia

image.caption: A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro RiverImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday vowed to continue hitting Russia's oil refineries in retaliation for what he called Moscow's new strategy of targeting major Ukrainian cities for intensive air strikes.
Ukraine has accused the Kremlin of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent days, to force residents to leave urban areas of the country before winter.
In strikes over the past two days, Russian forces have also hit two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in the capital, Kyiv.
What did Zelenskyy say?
In an interview with Reuters news agency, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence agencies had uncovered details of a "new doctrine" from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelenskyy warned.

The Ukrainian leader said that Kyiv would "respond in any way (we can) ... First of all, oil refiners: who give money to them [Russia] for this war. But we will not respond, of course, like them, on any ‌civilian objects."
Second Kyiv bridge struck
This week marks the first time Moscow has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday that the Northern Bridge over the river was struck by Russian forces from the air.
In a statement posted on Telegram, Klitschko said two people were injured and the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged.
"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.
Over the past two days, Kyiv's Southern Bridge has been hit several times by a volley of strikes by Russian drones.
The attacks caused traffic chaos, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

blocks.caption: Cars were stuck in traffic jams on Friday after Russian attacks on the Southern BridgeImage: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

blocks.text: A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.
Russia urges foreign diplomats, nationals to leave Kyiv
Russia's Foreign Ministry on Saturday, meanwhile, warned foreign diplomats and nationals in Kyiv to leave the city, adding that "individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger."

"The Armed Forces of the Russian Federation will continue to deliver massive retaliatory strikes," it said, while adding that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning."
In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.
Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.
Putin on a war footing: escalation on all fronts?
Moldova denounces latest Russian strike on Ukraine
Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the latest Russian attack on Kyiv and complained about a violation of her country's airspace.
"Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu said in a post on X. "5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil."
"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," Sandu said.
The Moldovan Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and urged Moscow to prevent such incidents.
Moldova is a strong supporter of Ukraine, and its airspace is frequently violated due to Russian attacks on its neighbor.
Russian forces are stationed in the Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria, raising fears that Moldova could be the next target of invasion after Ukraine.

articles.title: US Coast Guard searches for missing air ambulance off coast of Massachusetts
articles.summary:
The plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contact

The US Coast Guard is searching for an air ambulance jet with six people onboard that…

blocks.text: The US Coast Guard is searching for an air ambulance jet with six people onboard that lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during a flight from Bermuda to Boston early on Saturday morning.
In a statement to the Guardian, an FAA spokesperson said that the agency issued a search-and-rescue alert notice for a Gulfstream G-100 at about 1.20am local time on Saturday.

The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers onboard when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade international airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport, obtained by the Associated Press.

NBC News reported that the plane was carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda, citing a statement from Clarence Togeretz, the director of flight operations at Latitude Air Ambulance, the aircraft’s operator.

“We always get rather concerned when our crew doesn’t report to us in a timely manner,” he told NBC News. “But I will say that again, optimistically and positively, that doesn’t mean that the worst has happened.”

NBC also reported that the Massachusetts port authority, which operates Boston Logan international airport, said the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled. A port authority spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with those onboard and their loved ones as the search continues.”
The FAA is coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the US Coast Guard to locate the aircraft.
The search area as of Saturday morning was off the coast of the island of Nantucket, Massachusetts, the coast guard said in a statement posted to X.
Air and surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft, the statement added.
Citing a source with knowledge of the investigation, ABC News reported there were no Americans onboard the plane, though the identities of those onboard were not immediately released.
Officials believe the plane rapidly descended 7,500ft before hitting the water, according to the outlet’s source.

articles.title: 4 Canadians aboard missing Ontario-based air ambulance flying from Bermuda to Boston

blocks.text: Air ambulance went missing early Saturday
The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for an Ontario-based air ambulance jet that has gone missing with six people on board while flying from Bermuda to Boston on Saturday.
The Gulfstream G100 jet with tail number C-GRJP is registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, a Hamilton-based air ambulance provider, according to the tracking website Flightradar24.

The company lost contact with the jet around 1:30 a.m.today, said Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude. The U.S. Coast Guard's northeast division said the Federal Aviation Administration also reported losing contact with the jet in the early hours of Saturday.

There were two pilots and two medical staff — all of whom are Canadian — on board. A patient and their relative were also on board. They are not Canadian and were picked up in Bermuda, Togeretz told CBC.
Togeretz said they are staying optimistic that everyone will be safely found.
Air and surface teams are searching for the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., the U.S. Coast Guard's northeast division said in a social media post.

The jet's last trip was from Hamilton to the North Atlantic island of Bermuda on Friday evening, according to flight history on Flightradar24. Before Friday and Saturday's flights, the jet had flown within Canada over the past week.
CBC News has contacted federal and provincial authorities for more information about the aircraft.

articles.title: Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution, governor says
articles.summary: Pike survived two lethal injections on Wednesday and is currently in critical condition in hospital.

blocks.text: The head of prisons in the US state of Tennessee is set to resign after the failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike on Wednesday.
Governor Bill Lee announced the change on Saturday, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada said in a statement to CBS that his stepping down is "in the best interests" of the state, and called the ongoing investigation into the incident "entirely appropriate and necessary".

Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived two lethal injections and is now in critical condition at a Tennessee hospital as her lawyers seek to commute her sentence.

articles.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
articles.summary: The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

image.caption: Police forces across the UK have stepped up patrols outside synagogues [FILE: October 2, 2025]Image: Andrew Matthews/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.
The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.
What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, in northern England.
He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.
The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.
Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.
He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.
The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.
One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.
The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.
Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

blocks.caption: Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025]Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.
Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.
The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.
Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.
UK releases air base plot suspects

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.
UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.
Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.
The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.
Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.
Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title: ICC allows written testimony vs Duterte
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court has allowed the prosecution to introduce as evidence a prior testimony of one of its witnesses against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: October 4, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo
MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court has allowed the prosecution to introduce as evidence a prior testimony of one of its witnesses against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

In a 15-page decision released on Friday, the ICC Trial Chamber III granted the prosecution’s first request to introduce the prior written testimony of the witness identified in the filings as “P-1100.”
“[The Chamber] is satisfied that the substance of P-1100’s evidence and the reports he produced appear relevant to the background and context in this case,” the ruling read.

It rejected the defense’s opposition to the request, saying the witness testimony will not be offered as expert evidence and there is no indication the prosecution will use it to support conclusions beyond his personal knowledge.
“The Chamber notes that witnesses often provide conclusions or opinions while testifying in court as well as in written statements,” the judges ruled.

“Although P-1100’s prior recorded testimony contains some opinion statements, the defense will have the opportunity to question the witness, including to test the basis of P-1100’s knowledge, to probe the foundation for the interpretations he offers and to elicit the limits of what he is, and is not, able to say from personal observation,” it added.
Defense lawyer Peter Haynes earlier objected to the introduction of P-1100’s prior witness testimony, saying it “is neither sufficiently relevant nor probative of the facts in dispute in this case.”

In his original request, ICC acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang described the testimony as “relevant, reliable and probative.” He also said that it would streamline his in-court testimony during trial.
The judges agreed, but noted that the prosecution’s request for two hours to conduct a supplementary examination is excessive.
“The prosecution shall therefore streamline its questioning so as to complete its examination of P-1100 within one hour,” it added.
In its decision, the judges also authorized the prosecution to introduce five “associate materials” into evidence, although it rejected four others.
“This ruling does not prevent the defense from making use of any of the documents for the purpose of cross-examination,” said the judges.
Duterte’s trial is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30.

articles.title: Sara wants copy of ex-cop’s affidavit
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte wants to be provided first with a copy of the sworn affidavit of Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. before being required to face the National Bureau of Investigation to shed light on…

blocks.text: October 4, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte
AFP / Jam Sta. Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte wants to be provided first with a copy of the sworn affidavit of Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. before being required to face the National Bureau of Investigation to shed light on the allegations of the dismissed police officer that he delivered cash in suitcases to her and to some members of her family.
In a statement, Duterte’s counsel Paul Lawrence Lim confirmed that Duterte received an invitation from the NBI for a conference at 10 a.m. on Oct. 5 on Gracioso’s allegations.

“However, since no official copy of Mr. Gracioso’s affidavit was included with the invitation, we have requested the NBI for a faithful copy thereof and all its supporting documents, if any,” Lim said.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said they invited the Vice President to give her the chance to respond directly to Gracioso’s allegations.
The NBI will also invite Davao City 1st district Rep. Paolo Duterte, as well as former speaker Lord Allan Velasco and his wife, Rowena, who have not returned from a trip to Japan.
Matibag said the bureau wants to hear their denials and other explanations, particularly after some of those named by Gracioso claimed not knowing him.

“In your letter, you mention an ongoing investigation into allegations made by a certain Mr. Rodulfo M. Gracioso Jr. and request for our client’s statements, documents and records that may help clarify the issues at hand. However, while your letter mentions an attached copy of Mr. Gracioso’s sinumpaang salaysay, none was attached thereto. Consequently, our client cannot provide any meaningful reply to your request at this time,” Lim and other Duterte lawyers Clifford Chua and Kimberly Resurreccion said in their letter to Matibag.

They added that neither Duterte nor her counsels will appear before the NBI on Oct. 5, although they are willing to have their meeting moved to Oct. 8 “assuming our timely receipt of the requested documents.”
“Instead, we respectfully request that sufficient time be given our client and counsel to examine the sinumpaang salaysay and all accompanying documents to be provided her,” they said.

Gracioso, who served as part of Velasco’s security detail, earlier alleged that he also delivered cash-filled suitcases to her brother Paolo and father former president Rodrigo Duterte on Velasco’s instructions.

articles.title: Public urged to save water while supply remains steady
articles.summary: As the country faces what could be a super El Niño, consumers should save water while there is steady supply, National Water Resources Board executive director Sevillo David Jr. said yesterday.

blocks.text: October 4, 2026 | 12:00am

A resident fetches water from a manual pump along Macaraig Street in Manila on October 3, 2026. To prepare for the possible effects of a strengthening El Niño, authorities have urged the public to conserve water while there is still steady supply.
Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — As the country faces what could be a super El Niño, consumers should save water while there is steady supply, National Water Resources Board executive director Sevillo David Jr. said yesterday.
David said the demand for water is high especially during the dry season and they are expecting this as early as this year.
The country is facing a “very strong” El Niño this month, which may extend until the first half of 2027.

“Let’s be responsible in using water. As of right now, the supply is steady and we can give what the people need but it’s good that we trim our water consumption so what we can save will be used for the next months,” he said in an interview with One News.
David said they have issued water conservation measures to reduce the demand for water.
“When the demand is low, it can help manage the supply, particularly in the time when we can’t rely on rain water due to the ‘very strong’ El Niño,” the official said.
“We should not brush off the effects of El Niño, especially on water supply,” he added.
David said they are coordinating with local government units and other government agencies should the water supply go lower in the coming months.
He also discouraged consumers from hoarding and panic-buying water as it affects water distribution and supply.
“We have enough supply. Use your drums to catch rainwater and use it for other daily (activities) like flushing toilets. Using drums can help in catching water that dams cannot get,” he said.

articles.title: Woman, 2 children dead after serious collision near Foam Lake, Sask.
articles.summary: A serious car crash left three people dead and four others injured. A 40-year old man from South Carolina was arrested and charged.

image.caption: RCMP have charged a 40-year-old man from South Carolina after the crash. (Charles Contant/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·Updated
A serious car crash left three people dead and four others injured. A 40-year old man from South Carolina was arrested and charged.
40-year-old man from Sumter, South Carolina, was arrested and charged
A serious collision near Foam Lake, Sask., Friday afternoon has left three people dead.

On Friday afternoon, a truck was attempting to pass a semi and collided with an SUV on a grid road about nine kilometres west of Foam Lake, RCMP said in a Saturday news release. Foam Lake is about 150 kilometres northeast of Regina.
A 40-year old woman, an eight-year old girl and a five-year old girl, all from Foam Lake, were in the SUV and were declared dead at the scene by EMS.
An adult man was also in the SUV and was taken to hospital by STARS with serious injuries, the release said.

The driver of the truck was taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and two passengers were also taken to hospital. One passenger had non-life-threatening injuries, according to EMS, while the other had serious injuries, according to STARS, the release said.
The semi driver not not report any physical injuries to police and his semi was not damaged.

RCMP say 40-year-old Kelly Knopf from Sumter, South Carolina, was arrested and charged with three counts each of dangerous operation of a vehicle causing death and dangerous operation of a vehicle causing bodily harm.
He is scheduled to appear in Yorkton Provincial Court on Monday.
Wadena/Foam Lake RCMP continue to investigate with the assistance of a Saskatchewan RCMP collision reconstructionist.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Randi LaRocque is a Métis woman working as a reporter with CBC Saskatchewan. She can be reached at randi.larocque@cbc.ca

articles.title: Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
articles.summary: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.

blocks.text: US authorities are searching for six people after a medical plane bound for Boston, Massachusetts went missing early Saturday morning.
The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC that it lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane and put out a search and rescue notice just after 1:00 local time (6:00 GMT).
An air and water search is underway off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, according to the US Coast Guard's Northeast District.

The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was slated to land at Boston's Logan International at 1:30 EDT (6:30 GMT).
According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).

articles.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
articles.summary: Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.

image.caption: The latest wave of protests emerged in response to the forced eviction of an elderly woman in MadridImage: Alejandro Martinez Velez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.
The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.

"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.
They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.

blocks.caption: Protesters demanded affordable housingImage: Javier Soriano/AFP

blocks.text: "What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.
Protests in dozens of cities
Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.
Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.
In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.
Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.

blocks.caption: Protesters filled the streets of the Spanish capitalImage: Juan Barbosa/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's next for the Spanish government?

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.
This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.
"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators held signs calling for 'a right to a roof' among other slogansImage: Javier Soriano/AFP

blocks.text: Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decion.
Sahcnez's office declined to comment on the reports.

articles.title: Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
articles.summary: A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity. But his remains have been in Greece for decades – and he is also claimed…

image.caption: A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identityImage: ArTo/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: The remains of one of Bulgaria's most important medieval rulers were set to arrive in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Saturday after decades of negotiations with neighboring Greece.

Czar Samuel ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, gradually extending his authority over a swathe of the Balkans as far south as Lake Ohrid, now in North Macedonia on the border with Albania.
But Samuel's rule was also characterized by conflict with the Byzantine Empire which ultimately defeated his army at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014.
Samuel is said to have died of shock when thousands of his defeated soldiers returned home having been blinded by order of Byzantine Emperor Basil II, known as Boulgaroktonos – the "Bulgar Slayer."

The Bulgarian lands fell under Byzantine rule four years later but Czar Samuel is still considered a symbol of Bulgarian national identity today, and his remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are set to be received with full state honors.

They are set to be flown to Sofia aboard a military aircraft accompanied by a fighter jet escort before a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.
Free trains to the capital are being provided for the occasion, with some 750 police on duty during the handover ceremony.
Through the ages in Sofia
Bulgaria: 'Czar Samuel unites us'

"These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors," said Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev at a ceremony held at Museum of Byzantine Civilization in Thessaloniki, Greece, ahead of the handover.
Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with their southern neighbor.

"If, in the past, Czar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us," said Radev. "He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger."
Greece hopes for return of Parthenon Marbles

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, speaking alongside Radev, acknowledged that the remains of Czar Samuel have "incalculable cultural and spiritual but also emotional value" for Bulgaria, adding: "The global community is re-evaluating its long-standing stance on protecting cultural heritage."
In return, Greece is set to receive 48 sentimental objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War.

Some prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have criticized the exchange as inadequate on the Bulgarian side, but Mitsotakis said he hoped Saturday's ceremony would bolster Greece's international campaign to return the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.

"This shift is embodied by today's initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation."
Greece: How the Jewish cemetery in Thessaloniki disappeared
Czar Samuel: does North Macedonia also have a claim?
However, Bulgaria is not the only country to claim Czar Samuel, who is also celebrated with a huge statue in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia.

"The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again [contested] between Skopje and Sofia!" declared the Albanian-language newspaper Koha, while Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another "battle over history."

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended that Samuel be presented as the head of a state that "most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire" – territory which is now North Macedonia.
"Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia," Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told the AFP news agency.

Indeed, history has been playing a major role in the run-up to this month's Bulgarian presidential election, with incumbent President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Radev, promoting a more neutral position between the European Union and NATO – both of which Bulgaria belongs to – and Russia.

"Radev is looking to attract the patriotic electorate," said analyst Bechev, adding that the return of the remains to Sofia "aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia."
Gen Z leads Bulgaria's mass anti-corruption protests

image.caption: The flooding wreaked havoc on the town of Madrigueras in Spain's Castilla-La Mancha regionImage: Eva Manez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Floods in the Spanish southeastern town of Madrigueras have killed an 102-year-old woman, regional authorities said.
Madrigueras, which has a population of around 4,000 residents, is located near the city of Albacete in the Spanish autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha.
Authorities said 90 people had to be rescued due to flooding in the town.
Local Spanish media said the elderly woman was found dead in her home after the floodwaters had reached a depth of one meter (3.2 feet).
The floods in the region were caused by persistent torrential rainfall on Friday. Spanish authorities said around 140 liters of rainfall per square meter came down in Madrigueras.

blocks.caption: The flooding in Madrigueras also damaged vehicles in the town Image: Eva Manez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sanchez: Spanish government monitoring flood situation

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, in a post on X, said his government is monitoring the situation. He also expressed his regards to the family of the woman who died in the flooding in Madrigueras.
Spanish meteorological authorities said heavy rainfall is expected to continue in eastern Spain through Sunday.
The torrential rain and flooding comes after the Mediterranean country witnessed its hottest summer on record this year.
Deadly wildfires were reported in Spain's north and south in recent months due to frequent hot, dry conditions.

articles.title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
articles.summary: More than 50 protests are planned to take place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.

blocks.text: The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenant's Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

articles.title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
articles.summary:
Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down

Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell”…

blocks.text: Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.
But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.

Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.

blocks.caption: Khalifa Haftar. Photograph: Esam Omran Al-Fetori/Reuters

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.

Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”

But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.

Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.

On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.

Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.

The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.

Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”
He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.
The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.

Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says
articles.summary: The man, who stabbed his fellow pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight, was reportedly barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns.

image.caption: A replacement Flydubai aircraft landed in Tel Aviv, carrying passengers from the flight on which a pilot stabbed another [Photo: September 30, 2026]Image: Gil Cohen-Magen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The co-pilot accused of stabbing his captain during Flydubai Flight 1073 was wielding a crash ax and attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack," UAE investigators said Saturday, according to Emirati state news agency WAM.
A crash ax is typically stored in the plane's cockpit for use in case of an emergency.
Western and Gulf officials cited by Reuters and AP news agencies named the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami. Emirati authorities have not publicly commented on his identity.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that he had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views.
The attack that took place on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has raised many questions about how the incident unfolded as well as about background checks in aviation hiring.
There were 182 people on board, including four pilots.
After the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane, two other pilots in the cabin took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Flydubai co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman over security concerns
The Wall Street Journal report said the co-pilot was hired by Flydubai despite the ban by Oman, allowing him to fly the jet on a sensitive route connecting the UAE and Israel.
Israel and the UAE, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.
The newspaper said it could not be determined whether Oman shared concerns about the pilot's radicalization with other countries or airlines.
The nature of his radicalization was also not clear.
US broadcaster CNN cited two sources saying the co-pilot was removed from a job at Oman's national airline last year over concerns about extremist views.
Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya, also citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday in a video statement that they know the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination" and intended to crash the jet.
Netanyahu also said they were also looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price."

The investigation is ongoing. A Gulf diplomat, in comments to AP, said authorities were attempting to find out whether the Omani co-pilot was a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."
Flydubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt

articles.title: Canada scores a dairy win on U.S. soil as farmers grumble about Trump's trade war
articles.summary: At the World Dairy Expo in Wisconsin, the political tension between Canada and the U.S. is — more or less — set aside as farmers from both sides of the border focus on their best bovines. But even…

image.caption: Alyson Doiron of Cap-Sante, Que., and her prize cow Ella at the World Dairy Expo in Madison, Wisc., on Sept. 27, upon winning the top prize at the International Junior Holstein Show. (Cowsmopolitan)

blocks.text: On the most elite stage in the world of competitive dairy, a Canadian teenager and her "favourite cow" scored two major wins while on U.S. soil.
Never heard of competitive dairy? Let me assure you, it's a really big deal. One win — let alone two — at the World Dairy Expo in Madison, Wisc., can be life changing for farmers and their cows.

It can boost the value of an animal by tens of thousands of dollars. Future offspring can become more valuable too. And of course, there's an element of national pride, especially when Canada and the U.S. are locked in a trade war.

Alyson Doiron, a 16-year-old high school student from Cap-Sante, Que., glows as she poses for photos with her aforementioned favourite cow — Arolene Dempsey Ella, who goes by "Ella" for short, was the five-year-old cow awarded the top prize at the International Junior Holstein Show.
"She's an easy cow to work with. We love her so much," Doiron told CBC News.

Doiron cheered and cried as she was given the prestigious honour on Ella's behalf, at the Expo on Sunday. Even though this is a global gathering, the actual competitions are between animals from Canadian and American farms, due to health and safety regulations.
"This means a lot to me," she said with a nod to her home province. "It just proves that in Quebec, the [cow] show is really really strong," she said.
The win on Sunday was just the start of a very big week for Doiron and Ella.
Sore point for some Americans

In the arena where the cows are judged, Canadian, American and Mexican flags hang in the rafters. It is a reminder, as constant as the smell of manure, that cross-border competition and co-operation are valued in this space.

"I think it's important for us to be here," said Brian Carscadden, the executive senior manager and part owner of Blondin Sires, a Quebec-based dairy company that has milk production and artificial insemination operations.
"If you think of the Westminster Dog Show, it's not unlike that. If you can win that, you've got a dog that's worth some money. It's the same here with your cow."

Carscadden and his team drove more than 1,500 kilometres from St. Placide to Madison, with 25 cows in trailers in tow. He says his business has not been affected by the trade war yet, and that it does not come up often in conversations at the Expo.
"There's jokes here and there," from his American friends, he said, along with "the odd snide remark … that makes things interesting."
"I always advise my Canadian colleagues that it's not our country, it's not our politics, don't talk about it."
Americans at the Expo are far more direct.
The trade war is a sore point for some, including voters who are connecting dots between U.S. President Donald Trump's broad economic agenda and increases in the cost of living.
"There is no lowering of grocery prices, no lowering of gas prices. I mean obviously it's all going higher and it makes me struggle," said Paula Lawver.

She's a single mom from a farming community in Indiana, and is at the Expo with a group of students from her son's high school. She describes herself as a conservative voter with conservative values, but does not consider herself a Republican.

She calls the dispute with Canada "nonsense," and says it will influence her vote in the midterm elections this November. Lawver says she will not support candidates in favour of tariffs and trade wars.
Seth Muck, a farmer from New York state, says he too may reconsider how he votes in the midterms.

He says in the past he's voted "hard, hard Republican, hard conservative." But after feeling the impact of Trump's global trade agenda, he's considering backing candidates with a "bit more moderate-type agenda."

Muck says his cash crops and farm inputs have been affected the most, noting that the price of fertilizer is double what he paid last year. Though he still holds out hope that economic conditions could improve.
"Perhaps it's going to take a bit … like ripping off a Band-Aid," he said.

Even among those willing to be more patient with Trump and his economic vision, CBC News did not find any Americans at this Expo supportive of the heated rhetoric that has upended the Canada-U.S. relationship.
"I think it's needless, pointless and childish. Both sides," said Gary Craugh, a retired farmer from Wisconsin.
'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms
Another retired farmer from Wisconsin, John Galgowski, says he's baffled by it all.
"I throw up my hands and go, 'Why are we doing this?'"
Galgowski does not support the Trump administration, and says the way the country has been run since Trump returned to office has only reaffirmed his position.
"It's just bad times," he said.
The way these voters described their experience is very different from how the Trump administration is framing the moment.

items: Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates
U.S. bans on imported Canadian motorcycle, dairy, alcohol products take effect as trade war drags on

blocks.text: About 120 kilometres from the Expo, in Milwaukee, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer hosted a gathering of G20 trade ministers, where he unapologetically advocated for the "America first" trade agenda, arguing that the strategy is working.
"American workers and their families are better off now than they were before President Trump took office," Greer said as he read from prepared remarks.
Greer's defence of the Trump administration's policies suggests there are no plans to change course anytime soon.
Which means the trade war with Canada is poised to grind on.
Ella's big day
Even if the country-to-country tensions won't go away, Canada did score one more win at the World Dairy Expo.
On Friday, Doiron proudly paraded Ella in front of the judges on the arena floor, competing for one of the week’s largest titles: Supreme Junior Show Champion.
It's a moment that almost didn’t happen. Doiron says she helped raise Ella, but when her parents unexpectedly sold the cow, she was devastated.
"I was so mad at my parents, because she was just the cow I liked," she said, recalling the way she loved all of Ella's spots as a kid.

Doiron was determined to be reunited with her favourite cow, and when the opportunity arose, she re-purchased Ella, despite objections from her parents. "I need to bring this cow home," she told her mom.
The reunion was clearly meant to be.
In front of a packed arena, Doiron and Ella’s big moment finally arrived — the cow was named Supreme Junior Show Champion, a victory for all of Canada.

articles.title: With celebs and influencers glamourizing 'cigs' online, experts are carefully watching smoking trends
articles.summary: Social media is filled with images of celebrities and influencers lighting up cigarettes and hyping the habit of smoking, suggesting it's experiencing a bit of a cultural resurgence. Though data…

image.caption: Images of celebrities, influencers and other content creators smoking are all over social media, and experts warn that they can have an outsize influence on young people picking up the deadly habit. (Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Health·New

Social media is filled with images of celebrities and influencers lighting up cigarettes and hyping the habit of smoking, suggesting it's experiencing a bit of a cultural resurgence. Though data suggests tobacco use has long been trending downward, experts say if we want it to stay that way, harmful online content that glamourizes smoking shouldn't be ignored.
Experts say online content glamourizing cigarettes is harmful and no amount of smoking is safe
Dua Lipa in the streets of Italy. Charli XCX at her wedding. Singer Clairo snapping selfies. Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams out on the town.

These are just a few of the world's biggest celebrities who've recently appeared in dozens of photos on Instagram and TikTok, looking impossibly cool while doing something notoriously unhealthy: smoking cigarettes.
"It's almost like they're glamorizing smoking again," said Carolyn Baglole, an associate professor with McGill University's department of medicine.

But even with celebrities caught puffing and influencers hyping the habit, data suggests tobacco use has long been trending downward. Still, if we want it to stay that way, experts say online content glamourizing the habit shouldn't be ignored.
Global study found many people don't understand the dangers of smoking
No amount of smoking is safe: experts
Dedicated accounts to smoking culture have popped up online, including @cigfluencers, which boasts more than 100,000 followers on Instagram and posts pictures of celebrities smoking.
Meanwhile, posts normalizing "cigs" abound online.

Like the one that jokingly declares cigarettes don't count if you smoke them with your morning coffee or overseas. In another video, a woman defends influencer Alix Earle for smoking a cigarette with the caption, "Let a girl smoke a cheeky cig!" In another, the content creator says cigarettes don't count "if you're in the middle of writing."
However, experts warn that this is the kind of behaviour that can lead to addiction.

items: Q&A: This doctor says he's seeing the harms of social media on youth
Health officials trying to tackle massive and 'tragic' use of vapes among teens

blocks.text: "Nicotine is so highly addictive," said Rob Cunningham, a senior policy analyst with the Canadian Cancer Society. "A small number of cigarettes can lead to addiction and cravings."

According to Health Canada, tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of premature death in the country, and can lead to more than 40 debilitating and potentially fatal illnesses, including cancers and heart disease.

That hasn't stopped some people from posting about trends like "social smoking" — the practice of only smoking with friends or peers — while others even claim that smoking could "cure the loneliness epidemic" or help people make friends.
Though some of these posts may be facetious or played off as jokes, experts told CBC News no amount of smoking is safe.

"Even smoking socially, you don't want to risk a nicotine addiction," Baglole said. "If that happens and you become a life-long smoker, the risk of developing a chronic disease such as lung cancer, is so much higher."
Jared Oviatt is a smoker who runs the @cigfluencers account. Despite the popularity of his content, he previously told CBC Life that he doesn't believe we're in a smoking renaissance.
“I don’t see the comeback of cigarettes in celebrity culture as a true return to smoking as a mainstream habit,” Oviatt said.
“Are we seeing it more often? Yes. However, I also think we’re already nearing the peak of that trend."
Smoking on a downward trend
Cunningham confirmed that smoking isn't on the rise, at least not yet.
"So far, we have not seen an increase in smoking and that's good," he said.

Recent data from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health shows a significant downward trend between 1999 and 2025. For students in grades 7-12 in Ontario, smoking tobacco cigarettes decreased from 28.4 per cent in 1999 to 3.5 per cent by 2025.

items: Drinking among Gen Z adults has gone up, busting the sober myth
New data shows 1 in 3 young Canadians have tried nicotine pouches

blocks.text: According to the federal government, smoking rates have steadily declined across the country. About 300,000 Canadians who smoked in 2023 reported that they quit smoking in 2024, with just 11 per cent of adult Canadians reporting smoking that year.
"We want to keep that trend going downward," Baglole told CBC News. "I would hate to see that trend reversed in any way and in any age demographic. Smoking is just so bad for you."
U.K. lawmakers approve lifetime tobacco ban for anyone born in 2009 or after
Cunningham says the habit damages teeth, skin and causes bad breath.
"It's also very costly once you're addicted," he said. In Canada, a pack of cigarettes can cost anywhere from $14 to $26 Cdn.

items: U.K. lawmakers approve lifetime ban on sale of cigarettes, vapes to anyone born after 2008
A 'smoke-free generation' tobacco ban is coming to the U.K. Could it also happen in Canada?

blocks.text: He also warned that the content on social media that glamourizes smoking is harmful.
"The positive depictions by influential people on social media is extensive and concerning," he said.
"Actors or influential people or celebrities do have influence — outsized influence — on the people they're exposed to."
Cunningham says he believes celebrities and influencers have a responsibility to protect their fans.
"They wouldn't want their kids or grandkids to smoke, and they should realize their behaviour can influence vast numbers of young people."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Anya Zoledziowski is a Peabody-winning multimedia journalist from Edmonton who's covered social and climate justice, Indigenous affairs, gender, politics and more, and has been recognized by several national and international awards. She’s currently pursuing her PhD in journalism studies.
With files from Trevor Risk

articles.title: Internal documents show why Ottawa is worried about the Alberta referendum, even if the province votes to stay

image.caption: Alberta separatists rally outside the offices of Elections Alberta in May. Documents obtained by CBC News show the potential risks that the federal government is evaluating ahead of this month's referendum. (Todd Korol/ Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Internal federal documents offer insights into how Ottawa is assessing the economic fallout from the possibility of Alberta separating from Canada and becoming an independent state.
Briefing notes outline potential fiscal shocks, population outflows, head office exodus
The documents from Finance Canada and the Justice Department also shed light on the consequences being considered from the uncertainty caused by Alberta separatism.

Finance Canada briefing notes, released to CBC News through access to information legislation, detail the federal government has been quietly studying the impact of a possible $18-billion fiscal shock, corporate head office flight and a mass exodus of Albertans to neighbouring provinces if Alberta exits the federation.
It also flags that federal pension laws are "flawed" and might not be up to the task of dealing with the possibility of Alberta exiting the Canada Pension Plan.
Much of the documents were redacted but still shed light on a range of outcomes the government is considering this fall.
The documents are dated June 2026.

Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum asks voters whether the province should remain in Canada or hold another vote at a future date to leave. Up until now much of the analysis of the economic hit of Alberta potentially separating has focused on the impact on the province instead of Canada as a whole.
Although polling indicates more Albertans want to remain in Canada than leave, the documents show even the possibility of a separation referendum could cause economic harm to Canada and the province.
Exodus of business headquarters
The analysis invokes the 1995 Quebec referendum which resulted in Quebecers voting to remain in Canada by a tight margin.
Data from bond and equity markets showed that vote coincided with "tightening in financial conditions both provincially and nationally," it states.
Businesses, it notes, delayed "investment decisions pending greater clarity regarding future economic arrangement."

items: Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favours separation
Everything you need to know about the Alberta referendum

blocks.text: Citing data from the Conseil du patronat du Québec during the late 1970s and early 1980s, it states that 263 major corporate head offices, including Sun Life, left Montreal.
"Lingering uncertainty in Alberta could trigger a similar exodus of headquarters, especially for non-resources sector companies," the documents state.

Under the heading "interprovincial population outflow," it notes that in 2021 Alberta saw nearly 17,500 net workers with post-secondary degrees move into the province — and suggests highly educated and highly skilled workers would leave an independent Alberta in large numbers.
CBC News asked Finance Canada for more details about the department's work studying the impact of the Alberta referendum.

Instead, the Privy Council Office responded with an emailed statement which said the federal government is "conducting its own study of various third-party economic analyses" on the potential costs of Alberta's separation from Canada.

"Alberta is an integral part of Canada and contributes significantly to the prosperity of Albertans and Canadians. Alberta is stronger as part of a united Canada," wrote Privy Council spokesperson Mélany Gauvin.
15% of national GDP
The analysis is also a reminder of how much the Albertan economy provides for the rest of Canada.
Between 2022 and 2024, Alberta's net fiscal contribution averaged roughly $18 billion annually.
With the province accounting for $475 billion in annual economic activity, Alberta represents 15 per cent of national GDP over the last decade.
Over the same time period the province also accounted for 31 per cent of Canada's exports. Most of this came from energy.
Stability or a fair shake: Ranchers' perspectives on separation

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe has completed a similar analysis on the impact of separation. Tombe, who is part of the federalist group Lead Not Leave, notes that in 2024 Ottawa collected more than $19 billion than it spent in the province.

An independent Alberta would get to keep that money but Tombe's report found it would be quickly eaten up by NATO defence commitments, expenses related to assuming federal operations and falling revenues from a shrinking economy.

items: Establishing independent Alberta could cost up to $170B over 5 years: report

blocks.text: In an interview with CBC News, Tombe said although Canada stands to lose a lot from Alberta leaving, the real loser would be his province.
"Without doubt, it would be Alberta that would experience the largest economic disruption as a result of separation," Tombe said.
Canada Pension Plan impacts
Tombe has also done some number crunching on the impact of Alberta exiting the Canada Pension Plan.
The CPP was established in 1966 as a measure to provide retirement income to older Canadians and to make up for gaps in private pensions.

The plan has opt-out provisions and a formula to transfer assets, but the internal document notes the federal government's independent overseer of the CPP, the chief actuary, is concerned about the wording and payout formula set out in the federal law that governs the pension plan.
"In addition to the legislation being open to interpretation, the chief actuary has indicated that the formula it sets out is flawed," the documents state.

items: What to expect when you’re voting in the Alberta referendum and watching results

blocks.text: When the CPP and the legislation that came with it was set up in the 1960s, its assets were invested in provincial bonds.
But now the fund is invested in infrastructure like airports, equities and other global bonds — making divesting Alberta's share complicated.

"I would anticipate that if a province were to want to exercise their right to withdraw that the Supreme Court would have to make a ruling on what the language in the act ultimately means," Tombe said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: Canada bet billions on an EV boom. Was it too much, too soon?
articles.summary: The federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. But major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been…

image.caption: The steel frame of PowerCo's battery plant rises from the construction site in St. Thomas, Ont. Volkswagen's battery subsidiary now says production at the plant will begin in 2029, two years later than originally planned. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

The federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. But major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been delayed, cancelled, suspended, substantially changed — and in one case, gone bankrupt — as automakers and suppliers adjust to weaker-than-anticipated demand.
Volkswagen battery plant in Ontario latest major project to be delayed
The latest is Volkswagen's massive PowerCo battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., where production has been pushed back two years to 2029, because of "evolving market demand."

The setbacks are raising questions about whether Canada bet too big on how quickly the EV market would grow. Critics say demand may never reach the levels needed to support the scale of battery production governments sought to attract, while others argue these are temporary delays in the decades-long shift toward electrification.
A million batteries, but for what?

Grieg Mordue, a former Toyota executive and retired McMaster University professor who studied the auto industry, says the St .Thomas plant illustrates two problems with Canada's EV investment strategy: scale and location.
When the project was announced in 2023, PowerCo said the plant would eventually make enough battery cells for roughly one million EVs a year.

Mordue says that seemed inefficient since Volkswagen's major assembly operations are in the southern United States and Mexico, meaning batteries produced in St. Thomas would have to travel long distances to reach the vehicles they're intended to power.
Europe isn't the obvious destination either, he says, because Volkswagen (VW) already has battery production capacity there.
Even together, VW's North American plants don't produce enough vehicles to provide an obvious market for a million batteries a year.
"They got a million batteries," he said. "What are they going to do with them?"
VW and its PowerCo subsidiary did not respond to a request for comment.
VW has said the plant remains a cornerstone of its North American battery strategy and is continuing construction even as it pushes production back.
VW also said the delay will allow it to incorporate newer battery technology and scale production as demand develops.
It could also have an upside for taxpayers, Mordue said — in the form of a smaller subsidy bill.

Much of the support promised to Volkswagen is still tied to how many batteries the plant produces. With production now set for 2029 and with those incentives scheduled to start declining in 2030 and ending in 2032, Mordue says governments will likely pay "a whole lot less" than the original maximum.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said in a statement that the federal government has so far contributed $700 million to the construction of the St. Thomas battery plant, noting Ontario is responsible for one third of the $13.2 billion governments have agreed to in production subsidies.
"The government remains engaged with PowerCo on their updated timelines," the statement said.
Ontario's Ministry of Economic Development Job Creation and Trade did not respond by deadline.
A bet on the long-term
Still, others argue that looking at today's EV demand misses the time scale on which investments such as St. Thomas were made.
"These investments are meant to last 50 to 70 years or more," Joanna Kyriazis, directory of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada told CBC News.
She said the current slowdown should be seen as growing pains in an industry that is still transitioning, rather than evidence Canada built too much battery capacity.
There are signs Canada's EV market may already be recovering after a slowdown.

New restgistrations of battery-only EVs rose 37.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same time last year, according to Statistics Canada. When hybrids are included, Canadians registered 58,811 new zero-emission vehicles during the quarter, up 26.7 per cent.
Kyriazis says the investments are about keeping Canada relevant as the global auto industry undergoes a historic shift from gasoline-powered vehicles.
"It's not a question of maintaining a place in the North American auto indstury. It's — is Canada going to have an auto industry that survives in the 21st century at all?" she said.

"There's a clear direction that the global auto sector is going and if Canada wants to have a competitve auto sector into the future, we've got to be able to make and sell competitively priced electric vehicles and the parts that go into them."

Kyriazis says the potential market for these batteries also extends beyond electric vehicles. As electricity grids expand, batteries will increasingly be needed to store power and help balance supply and demand.

items: Gas prices and new incentives sparking more EV sales
Gas prices are dropping. You can thank the 'winter blend' for that

blocks.text: The St. Thomas site and a NextStar plant in Windsor, she said, "were looking at a short-term strategy of building batteries that would be used for grid-scale storage while EV update in North American started to sort of even out."

Kyriazis argues the current U.S. retreat from electric vehicles could prove temporary and that Canada shouldn't base a decades-long industrial strategy on policies that could change again under a future administration.
There is evidence the EV battery bet may have been early rather than fundamentally misplaced. The wider justification for building domestic battery capacity hasn't disappeared either.

China produced more than 80 per cent of the world's battery cells last year, according to the International Energy Agency, leaving governments in North America and Europe to build domestic supply chains in an industry that remains heavily concentrated in Asia.
Will buyers catch up?

University of Guelph economics professor Ross McKitrick is less convinced that time will solve the problem. He said EVs have an established market, but argues governments built their policy around expectations of demand far greater than what has so far emerged.
"What the government's been trying to do is force that market into existence," he said. "The numbers just don't add up."

McKitrick points to the billions governments offered manufacturers to build EVs and batteries, while simultaneously offering consumers incentives to buy the vehicles as evidence the industry wasn't able to sustain itself on the scale governments envisioned.

In a 2024 paper published in the Canadian Journal of Economics, McKitrick warned that if Canada's EV sales requirements rise faster than buyers' willingness to purchase them, it could hurt automakers and the wider economy.

items: Want to buy a used EV? Here’s what to look out for
As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

blocks.text: Ottawa scrapped EV sales requirements in 2026 and is moving repeal the broader federal mandate. It announced replacement emissions standards in February with consultations on the proposed regulations running until October 29.
Electric vehicles still account for a minortiy of new vehicle sales in Canada, despite years of government incentives aimed at encouraging consumers to buy them.
Electric vehicles accounted for 11.7 per cent of new light-duty vehicle sales in Canada in the first three months of 2026, according to Transport Canada, down from a peak of 15.4 per cent in 2024.
"At this point, it's a niche market," McKitrick said. "Some households like the product and are willing to pay for it."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Colin Butler is based in London, Ont., where he reports for Ontario and national audiences. He covers investigative, science, public policy and government accountability with a particular interest in using public records to uncover hidden stories.
